title: Connect prism-pyramid and cylinder-cone volume
learning_goals: Compare solids with the same base area and perpendicular height to identify volume relationships.
Explain and use the one-third volume relationship between a prism and pyramid or a cylinder and cone with matching base and height.
Connect experimental, tabular, and formula evidence while keeping base area, height, and units explicit.
success_criteria: I match solids by equal base area and perpendicular height before comparing volume.
I explain why the pyramid or cone volume is one third of the corresponding prism or cylinder volume.
I calculate and verify volumes in cubic units and distinguish a demonstration from a proof.

vocabulary.meaning: the two-dimensional area of the selected base used in a three-dimensional volume formula
the shortest distance from a base plane to the opposite face or vertex, measured at right angles to the base
a solid with congruent parallel bases and a constant cross-sectional relationship along its height
a solid with a polygonal base whose triangular faces meet at one vertex
a solid with a circular base that narrows to one vertex, with volume one third of a matching cylinder when base and height are equal

why_it_matters: Volume formulas become easier to remember and check when they are connected rather than treated as unrelated rules. Packaging, tanks, hoppers, roofs, moulds, piles, and 3D models often compare solids that share a footprint and height but hold very different amounts.

direct_instruction.heading: Match the comparison conditions
direct_instruction.body: Before claiming a one-third relationship, verify that the two solids have the same base area and the same perpendicular height. A cone with a different radius or a pyramid with a different base cannot be compared by the simple one-third statement. Label the base and height explicitly on both solids.

direct_instruction.heading: Use experiment as evidence, not magic
direct_instruction.body: A physical or simulated fill experiment can compare a pyramid with a matching prism or a cone with a matching cylinder. Repeatedly transferring the smaller solid's contents suggests that three equal smaller volumes fill the larger one under the matching conditions. The experiment builds intuition, while a full geometric proof requires reasoning beyond a few measurements.

direct_instruction.heading: Connect the formulas
direct_instruction.body: A prism or cylinder with base area B and height h has volume Bh. The corresponding pyramid or cone has volume one third Bh. For a circular base, B = πr², so a cylinder is πr²h and a cone is one third πr²h. Keep cubic units and delay rounding until the final step.

method_routes.title: Same-base-and-height comparison experiment route
steps: Choose or draw a prism-pyramid pair or cylinder-cone pair with equal base area and perpendicular height.
Measure and record the shared dimensions and estimate expected volume order.
Use a safe fill, digital simulation, or supplied data to compare how many smaller-solid volumes make the larger solid.
Record repeated measurements and sources of error rather than forcing an exact result.
Connect the observed ratio to the formulas Bh and one-third Bh and state the limits of experimental evidence.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route to build intuition for the one-third factor through a measurable comparison before relying on the symbolic formula.
method_routes.check: The paired solids must actually share base area and perpendicular height, and experimental error must not be presented as exact proof.

method_routes.title: Formula-and-scaling analysis route
steps: Calculate or identify the base area B with correct square units.
Identify the perpendicular height h and confirm it is not a slanted edge.
Compute the matching prism or cylinder volume Bh.
Multiply by one third for the corresponding pyramid or cone and write cubic units.
Compare the two results, verify the 3:1 ratio, and test how a changed radius, base, or height would affect both.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route for exact or symbolic calculations and for comparing how the same changed dimension affects related solids.
method_routes.check: The formula must use base area rather than a raw side length, the height must be perpendicular, and the final ratio should be three to one under matched conditions.

representations.label: Matched solid diagrams
representations.description: A prism and pyramid or cylinder and cone are drawn with equal base dimensions and perpendicular heights marked so the comparison conditions are visually explicit.
representations.text_alternative: State the two solid types, shared base dimensions and base area, shared perpendicular height, each formula, each volume, and the resulting three-to-one relationship.

representations.label: Volume comparison table
representations.description: Rows list base area, height, Bh reference volume, one-third factor, calculated volume, units, experimental estimate, and observed-to-formula difference.
representations.text_alternative: Read the common base area and height first, then the larger-solid volume, smaller-solid factor and volume, experimental result if used, and error or rounding note.

worked_examples.prompt: A cylinder and cone both have radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm. Compare their volumes.

steps.label: Find the common base area
steps.explanation: B = π(3²) = 9π cm² for this geometric calculation.

steps.label: Calculate and compare the cone
steps.explanation: V_cone = one-third of 72π = 24π cm³, so the cylinder holds three cone volumes.

worked_examples.answer: The cylinder volume is 72π cm³ and the cone volume is 24π cm³; their ratio is 3:1.
worked_examples.verification: The solids share base area and perpendicular height, and the formulas preserve the exact one-third relationship.

worked_examples.prompt: A square-based prism and pyramid share a 6 cm by 6 cm base and height 10 cm. Predict what a fill comparison should show.

steps.label: Compute the reference volume
steps.explanation: Base area is 36 cm², so the prism volume is 36×10 = 360 cm³.

steps.label: Apply the relationship
steps.explanation: The matching pyramid volume is one third of 360, or 120 cm³.

steps.label: Predict the experiment
steps.explanation: Ignoring spill and measurement error, three full pyramid volumes should fill the prism exactly.

worked_examples.answer: The formulas predict 360 cm³ for the prism and 120 cm³ for the pyramid, so a careful fill comparison should be close to three pyramid fills per prism.
worked_examples.verification: The prediction follows matched base and height conditions and treats any fill discrepancy as experimental error rather than a new formula.

misconceptions.claim: Every cone has one third the volume of every cylinder.
misconceptions.correction: The one-third comparison requires the cone and cylinder to have the same base area and perpendicular height.

misconceptions.claim: The slanted side of a cone is its height.
misconceptions.correction: Volume uses the perpendicular distance from the base plane to the vertex, not the slant length.

misconceptions.claim: A fill experiment that is close to three proves the formula for all solids.
misconceptions.correction: A demonstration provides empirical support and intuition; a general proof requires mathematical reasoning beyond finitely many trials.

guided.prompt: A prism has base area 20 cm² and height 7 cm. What is its volume?
guided.rationale: Prism volume is Bh = 20×7 = 140 cubic centimetres.

guided.prompt: A pyramid matches that prism's base and height. What is its volume?
guided.rationale: A matching pyramid has one third of the prism volume.

guided.prompt: Explain the conditions required before saying a cone is one third of a cylinder's volume.

criteria: states equal base area or same radius
connects formulas Bh and one-third Bh
response.sample_response: The cone and cylinder must have the same circular base area, which can come from the same radius, and the same perpendicular height. The cylinder then has volume Bh while the cone has volume one third Bh, so only under those matched conditions is the cone exactly one third as large.

guided.rationale: The one-third ratio depends on shared geometric conditions, not merely on the solid names.

independent.prompt: A cone has radius 2 cm and height 9 cm. Give its exact volume.
Which measurement is the height in a pyramid volume formula?

options: the perpendicular distance from base to vertex
response.correct_answer: the perpendicular distance from base to vertex

independent.rationale: Volume uses perpendicular height because it measures separation between base plane and vertex.

independent.prompt: A matching cylinder has volume 300 mL. What is the cone volume?
independent.rationale: A matching cone has one third the cylinder volume.

independent.prompt: If a cylinder radius doubles and height stays fixed, by what factor does its volume change?
independent.rationale: The circular base area scales with radius squared, so volume changes by 2² = 4 when height is fixed.

independent.prompt: Compare a square prism and square pyramid with side 5 m and height 12 m.

response.sample_response: The common square base has area 25 m² and the perpendicular height is 12 m. The prism volume is 25×12 = 300 m³. The matching pyramid is one third of that, 100 m³, so the prism-to-pyramid volume ratio is 3:1.

independent.rationale: The calculation uses the same base area and height in both formulas and preserves cubic units.

retrieval.prompt: What symbol is often used for base area in V = Bh?
retrieval.rationale: B represents the two-dimensional area of the selected base.

retrieval.prompt: How many matching cone volumes fill a cylinder in the ideal geometric relationship?
retrieval.rationale: A matching cone has one third the cylinder volume.

retrieval.prompt: Why should a fill experiment record error instead of changing the formula to fit one trial?

criteria: distinguishes empirical trial from exact mathematical relationship
uses repeated trials or formula comparison
response.sample_response: A physical fill can lose material, trap air, or use imperfect models and measuring tools, so one result may be slightly above or below three. Record and repeat the measurements, then compare them with the exact formula relationship rather than altering the mathematics to match experimental noise.

retrieval.rationale: Measurement error belongs in the evidence record and does not justify changing a general formula.

reflection_prompt: Which part of the one-third relationship came from measured or simulated evidence, and which part came from the mathematical formula and matching-base-height conditions?

accessibility.nonvisual_route: Every 3D comparison is paired with a linear description naming base shape and area, perpendicular height, formulas, exact and approximate volumes, expected fill ratio, and experimental-error note.
